vignette: It happens on a Tuesday in November. Arthur walks home from the public library, his canvas tote heavy with paperbacks, when a man steps out from behind a parked delivery truck. There is no warning, no exchange of words. A gloved hand clamps over Arthur's mouth, yanking him backward into the alley. The pavement rushes up to meet his shoulder. Arthur fights, his cane skittering across the wet asphalt, but the man's knee drives into his lower back. Fingers rifle through Arthur's jacket pocket, snatch his wallet, and then drive a fist into the side of Arthur's head. When the attacker disappears around the corner, Arthur lies in the damp concrete, listening to his own ragged breathing and the distant hum of traffic. He does not call for help. He just walks home, pretending nothing happened. The quiet of his suburban house, which once felt like a sanctuary, now feels thin. Arthur sleeps on the guest room mattress on the floor, away from the door. At sixty-eight, he is used to being the steady presence in a room. Now, that steadiness fractures. When his wife, Clara, asks why he won't come to bed, he tells her his back is sore. He stops taking the evening walk to the grocery store. Instead, he leaves the house at dusk, when the streets are empty, and buys only what he needs. His hands tremble when he signs the receipt. At home, he checks the locks three times before dinner. He tells himself it is routine, that he is simply being careful, but his stomach tightens into a hard knot the moment he hears a car door slam. Arthur spent forty-two years as a school counselor. He knows how to name what is happening to him, how to explain hyperarousal to a trembling sophomore or help a teenager process grief. Naming it does not stop the shaking. When he returns to the high school where he once worked, now as a guest speaker for career day, he cannot sit in the faculty lounge. The fluorescent lights buzz with a frequency that makes his teeth ache. He finds himself scanning every exit, mapping escape routes before the principal even finishes speaking. During a Q&A session, a student's sudden chair scrape echoes like a gunshot. Arthur's breath catches. His vision tunnels. For three seconds, he is back on the wet concrete, waiting for the weight of a boot on his spine. He blinks, and the classroom is just a classroom. He finishes his talk by speaking slowly, deliberately, forcing his hands to rest flat on his knees. Now, Arthur sits in my office with his knees drawn up slightly, his posture coiled. The late afternoon light catches the dust motes dancing near the window, and he watches them with a kind of exhausted reverence. He speaks in measured sentences, but the pauses are long, heavy. He describes the way his marriage has shifted. Clara tries to maintain normalcy, cooking his favorite meals, suggesting they drive to the coast, but Arthur flinches when she reaches for his arm. He loves her fiercely, but intimacy feels like a vulnerability he can no longer afford. He sleeps in the master bedroom again, but he leaves the nightlight on. He wakes at 3:17 a.m. almost every night, heart hammering, convinced he hears footsteps on the porch. He tells himself it is just the wind, just the house settling, but his body does not believe him. Today, he traces the edge of his coffee mug with his thumb, his gaze fixed on the floor. He talks about the anger that surprises him most-not at the man who hurt him, but at his own body. It feels like a traitor, bracing for a blow that has not come. He mentions how he avoids crowded parking lots, how he keeps his back to the wall in restaurants, how he rehearses conversations in his head before dialing the phone. The world has narrowed to a perimeter of safe, predictable things. Yet, when he speaks about his students, about the quiet satisfaction of guiding someone through their own storms, something in his shoulders drops, just slightly. He leans forward. He stays. He does not know how to untangle the fear from the man he still is, but he keeps showing up, one Tuesday at a time.
